name: Low milk supply and feeding problems
one_line: Worrying about having enough milk is very common. Most mothers can make more with frequent feeds, a good latch and the right support.
who_this_is_for: Breastfeeding mothers who worry their baby is not getting enough milk, and families who want to help them.
red_flags: Very few wet nappies, or dark yellow urine after the first week
Baby very sleepy, hard to wake or too tired to feed
Dry mouth, or a sunken soft spot on the head
Yellow skin that is spreading or getting deeper
Fever with a red, hot, painful breast in the mother
doctor_questions: Is my baby gaining weight well for their age?
Can someone watch a feed and check my baby's latch?
How many wet nappies should I expect each day?
Could tongue tie or anything else be making feeding harder?
Is there a health reason, such as thyroid, affecting my supply?
Should I express milk, and how often?
If my baby needs top ups, how should I give them and keep breastfeeding?

track.label: Feeds and wet nappies, to share with your doctor

faq.q: How do I know my baby is getting enough milk?
faq.a: Steady weight gain, plenty of wet nappies and a baby who seems content after most feeds are good signs. After the first week, most babies have at least six heavy wet nappies a day. Your doctor will check your baby's weight at visits.

faq.q: Is it normal for my baby to feed very often?
faq.a: Yes. Newborns usually feed 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, and some evenings they feed again and again. This cluster feeding is normal and helps build your supply.

faq.q: How can I make more milk?
faq.a: Milk is made on demand: the more milk is removed, the more your body makes. Feed often, check the latch, offer both breasts and keep your baby skin to skin. A lactation consultant can help.

faq.q: Do special foods or herbs increase milk?
faq.a: Eating well and drinking to thirst are good for you, but no single food is a sure answer. Check with your doctor before taking any herb or medicine for milk supply. Frequent, effective feeding matters most.
Ask your paediatrician or gynaecologist for a lactation consultant. Many hospitals have one, and your local ASHA or ANM worker can also support you at home.
